# Why Glassdoor reviews remain relevant in 2025




This title was summarized by AI from the post below.















































Taylor Meadows








































9mo



Edited

5 reasons why Glassdoor reviews are still relevant in 2025 ⬇️ they:

1️⃣ Give employees a voice in our new "perfectly crafted" AI world
2️⃣ Help the next job seeker navigate their search transparently
3️⃣ Hold our employers accountable for promises they make
4️⃣ Put employee feedback directly in front of HR and leadership
5️⃣ Immediately validate or invalidate the story being sold

I find that I still look to (and filter by) reviews FIRST before pulling the trigger. Glassdoor, Amazon, Google, TrustPilot, OpenTable, App Store...

I think sites like Reddit, Fishbowl, Blind also offer conversational transparency but I still appreciate a quantifiable review.

Hmm what's your take on reviews these days? Glassdoor or otherwise?

The job market is flooded

AI mass-application tools lowered the bar, so many applicants started applying to everything.

It’s just too easy.



Candidates can fire off 100+ applications an hour.

But their generic applications don’t get noticed.

And they make it harder for truly good candidates to get seen.



Last month, a Y Combinator startup posted 8 roles.
23,000 applications arrived in 30 days.¹

That's 2,875 people fighting for one position.

Spotify opened a single NYC engineering role.
1,700 applications in 15 hours.

You might think hiring managers
Would be excited about so many candidates.

But they're not. They're drowning.

Here's what nobody's telling you:
It's harder than ever for hiring managers to find qualified candidates

Recruiters at major tech companies report that only 10% of their hires now come from inbound applications.¹



The majority come from direct outreach and referrals.

But here's the question that stops most people:
How do you find hiring managers?
And how do you reach them without seeming desperate?

This is where everything changes.

Because there's something that solves both problems at once.

THE 5-STEP FRAMEWORK THAT ACTUALLY WORKS

Step 1: Pick One Job Title

Not three. One.



Most people hedge their bets. "I'll apply to marketing manager, marketing coordinator, and brand strategist."



Bad move. Your resume can't serve three masters.



So find a job title that fits you like your favorite shirt.



Choose the exact title you want. Make it specific.





Step 2: Build the Resume That Matches

Your resume isn’t a master key.

It’s a key to a very specific lock.



Your resume should read like you already have the job you're applying for.



Use their language. Mirror their requirements.



That score measures what recruiters actually care about: relevance, clarity, and impact.

I still remember when Yahoo was the heart of the internet era.
Almost everyone had a Yahoo Mail, we used Yahoo Search every day, and Yahoo 360 was our early version of Facebook. Yahoo Messenger wasn’t just a chat app — it was part of our digital memory.
But after a few years, everything changed. Most of its services were abandoned, and Google became the king. Yahoo’s empire quietly faded away.
And the question is: who can say the same thing won’t happen again — this time in the AI era?

From Innovation to Irrelevance
In the previous article, I talked about how marketing and narrative are becoming more important than technology itself.
When technical barriers disappear, what remains is the story — how a company communicates meaning, trust, and purpose to people.
Yahoo wasn’t overtaken because it lacked engineers; it lost its narrative. It stopped being the place where people felt connected to the web. Google came with a clear story: “organizing the world’s information” — simple, bold, and memorable.
That’s the power of narrative.

Branding as the New Survival Skill
In the AI era, technology alone won’t guarantee survival. AI will soon automate content, code, design, even strategy.
What will matter most is how brands make people feel and what they stand for.
According to a 2024 Edelman Trust Barometer report, 71% of consumers say they buy from brands that reflect their personal values. Another study by McKinsey found that companies with strong brand purpose and consistent storytelling outperform their competitors by up to 400% in brand value growth.
So before building another AI feature, companies should ask:
What’s our story in this new world?
Do our customers — and our own employees — believe in it?
Are we still human, or just another tech provider in a sea of infinite products?

Looking Ahead
In the next article, we’ll explore how to evaluate a company’s internal and external narrative — and the signs that show whether it’s built to survive or vanish in this new AI-driven market.

Sam Altman says we’ll see a one-person billion-dollar company in 2026.

I think we’ll see a one-person burnout instead.

He’s not wrong about the tech being there. It is.

Cursor writes prod code. Claude handles ops workflows. Agents handle customer support.

The tech works.

But here’s what I think nobody is taking about: a billion-dollar company needs about 10,000 decisions per week to work. No exaggeration. Decisions like:
→ Product roadmap calls
→ Pricing strategy
→ Which features to kill and which to 2x
→ How to respond to that massive client
→ Who to hire

Instagram had 13 employees when it sold for $1B to Facebook. 769 decisions per person, per week split evenly.

Realistically? Keven Systrom probably made 3k+ himself each week.

But he had 12 humans to debate those decisions with. 12 people to say “actually, that’s a stupid idea” before committing.

Could one person make all 10,000 decisions on their own?

Even if AI handled 80% of the execution, you’d still be making 100s of strategic calls a week on your own. No cofounder to say “remember your last bright idea?” (shout out Dev for being my sparring partner everyday).

Decision fatigue is a judgement problem, not a productivity problem.

After 47 decisions and three cups of coffee on a Wednesday afternoon, you start looking for shortcuts. You start deferring to AI’s recommendation because you’re over capacity. You might even start accepting “done” in place of “right”.

In my opinion, the future isn’t one superhuman founder with only AI agents for employees. It’s small teams of exceptional humans using agents to feel like a team of 50. They can debate, disagree (super important), and catch blind spots.

It’s not a hot take - it’s just common sense.

Have you seen a founder try to do everything solo? Has it ever worked?

Every one of these lessons hits beyond product design — they apply to business, leadership, and even mindset. -

1️⃣ We’re living through a “habit-formation window.”
The next 12 months will define how people use AI for years ahead.
Just like how ChatGPT quickly became a reflex for millions, the habits being formed right now will decide who wins long-term.
Google realized early on that if users got comfortable finding AI answers elsewhere, they’d lose more than traffic — they’d lose behavior.

2️⃣ Clarity always beats cleverness.
The simplest words and most familiar icons outperform fancy ones.
When users instantly “get it,” adoption follows.
Even a small label change — from Favorites to Close Friends — can transform engagement.

3️⃣ Great products are born from healthy dissatisfaction.
The best builders are never content with “good enough.”
They notice the tiniest friction — a sticker that rips a fruit peel — and ask, why does it have to be this way?
That constant discomfort with the ordinary drives innovation.

4️⃣ When users hack your product, they’re giving you a roadmap.
Workarounds are gold.
Instagram users creating fake private accounts led to “Close Friends.”
People typing “AI” at the end of searches led Google to design “AI Mode.”
User improvisation = product direction.

5️⃣ Understand the emotional job, not just the feature request.
“Close Friends” wasn’t about lists — it was about connection.
The real insight came from observing when someone first decides to use it — that moment of intent reveals what they’re really hiring the product to do.

6️⃣ Small design details make familiar ideas feel native.
Instagram Stories worked not because they copied Snapchat, but because they refined it — camera roll uploads, a pause button, smoother tools.
When adding new features to mature products, let them have their own space rather than hijacking existing ones.

7️⃣ The ‘lean startup’ approach isn’t always the answer.
Being lean helps in early testing — but some breakthroughs need weight and patience.
The “Close Friends” feature took two years because the team stayed too small for too long.
Sometimes, speed comes from scale.

Stakeouts for Good: Why Watching Customers Matters More Than Ever

As a life-long researcher watching humans use technology, I think human behavior is changing faster than it has since the 90s.

I recently watched a woman shop online for a new product (a customer "stakeout").

For 45 minutes, she bounced between TikTok Shop and ChatGPT — asking for ideas, watching short reviews, comparing options.

She never opened Google.
She never checked Amazon.
She never visited a brand’s site.

That behavior didn’t exist a year ago.

We’re in the middle of a major shift in how people discover and decide — bigger than when we all stopped typing URLs and started Googling everything.

I would argue that this time, it’s happening faster.
If you’re only doing user research once in a while — tied to specific projects — you’ll miss the signals.

By the time you notice, your customers (and competitors) are already ahead.
It’s time to build an ongoing practice of ”stakeouts for good" — a way to continuously watch, listen, and learn from real people using your products and your competitors’.

Almost all companies are oriented around only studying one product or features within a product - not general user behavior in their space.

Without a higher-level understanding of how consumer (or business user) behavior is changing, companies will get caught flat-footed.

Human behavior isn’t just changing, it's accelerating. An always-on practice of watching human behavior through customer stakeouts for good is more essential than ever.

Have you noticed similar shifts in how fast your customers' and prospects' behavior is changing?

Vishal Manocha

Most people use Glassdoor the wrong way.
They check it after the interview...

After they’ve applied.
After they’ve prepared.
Sometimes even after they’ve accepted the offer.

And then they read the reviews.
“Work culture is bad.”
“High pressure team.”
“Leadership issues.”

And suddenly they think:
“Maybe I shouldn’t have applied here.”

But the question is…
Why did you check so late?

I remember speaking to a professional last month.
He had already gone through three interview rounds with a company.
Only then he opened Glassdoor.

He read the reviews.
And realised the exact problems he was trying to escape in his current job… existed there too.
Same long hours.
Same chaotic management.
Same burnout stories.

He told me:
“Sir, I wish I had checked this earlier.”
That’s the real use of Glassdoor.
Not curiosity.
Strategy.

Before you apply, understand three things:
What employees are saying.
What patterns repeat in reviews.
And whether the problems match what you want to avoid.
Because job search is not just about getting offers.

It’s about choosing the right environment.
And these are exactly the kind of practical conversations we have every week inside our Tuesday Q&A sessions.
Real career questions.
Real situations.
Real strategies.

Every Tuesday we sit together and break down things like:
Job search mistakes
Notice period traps
Interview strategy
Career growth decisions

If you want to join the next session,
Click the link in the pinned comments.

These Q&A sessions have become one of the most valuable spaces for professionals to learn things that nobody teaches in corporate life.

See you there next Tuesday.

“Why do you want to work here?”

If we’re being honest, this might be one of the most performative questions in the entire hiring process.

Most candidates land on a job posting for two very real reasons. Either they’re in a role they no longer want to be in, or they’re currently unemployed and need to get back to work. They’re searching for something that aligns with their skills, experience, and ability to contribute. Your posting showed up, it made sense, and they applied. That’s the truth in the vast majority of cases.

But the interview process rarely invites that kind of honesty. Instead, candidates feel pressure to craft an answer that flatters the organization, mirrors its mission statement, and signals some deep, pre-existing passion for the company. It turns into a moment where authenticity is replaced with performance, and both sides know it.

The reality is this. There’s nothing wrong with someone needing a job. There’s nothing wrong with someone wanting a better situation, better leadership, or a healthier environment. In fact, those are often the candidates who are most motivated to show up, contribute, and grow. What actually matters is whether the role fits their capabilities and whether they can add value once they’re in it.

If we want better hiring outcomes, we should be asking better questions. Questions like, “What kind of environment helps you do your best work?” or “What does a strong team look like to you?” or “What would make you successful here in your first six months?” Those answers tell you far more than a polished speech about why someone has always dreamed of working at your company.

Because if we created space for complete honesty, a lot more candidates would simply say, “I need a job.” And that wouldn’t be a red flag. That would be a starting point.

Most people ignore red flags in interviews because they are desperate for the job.
Here are the red flags to watch for and what to do when you spot them.

What to ask: "How do you maintain work-life balance in the team?"

𝗩𝗮𝗴𝘂𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻.
What it signals: High turnover or problematic role.
What to ask: "Why did the last person leave this position?"

𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝘄.
What it means: People do not stay long. Something is driving them away.
What to check: "How long has the team been working together?"

𝗝𝗼𝗯 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘀.
What it reveals: Lack of clarity or they are adding work they could not hire for separately.
What to do: Ask for written role clarity before final round.

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆.
What it signals: Either desperation or they are hiding something that makes people reject offers.
What to do: Always ask for at least 48 hours. Good companies give you time.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗻𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀.
What it shows: Toxic culture. They will do the same to you.
What to notice: Listen to how they talk about people who left.

𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗲𝘅𝗵𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗱.
What it means: This could be you in 6 months.
What to observe: Pay attention to energy levels of people working there.

One question that reveals everything:
"𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲?"
Short tenures across the board? Red flag.

What red flag have you ignored in an interview that you later regretted? Share yours below.

Mine: "We will define your role after you join." Spent 6 months doing work nobody else wanted to do.

When is the last time you printed out your résumé and actually walked through your experience before an interview?

What is one professional skill you realized you needed to improve later in your career, and what did you do to strengthen it?

Tip for the Day Series

Shout out to those getting it right!!

Today’s post is a small celebration for an employer whom (in my opinion) understands the importance of candidate feedback and how it can actually enhance your brand.

I don’t want to name the employer because I don’t want them to be bombarded with expectations from candidates going forward but instead want to share what they did and how they did it which made an impression on me.

When I left my last employer in Dec 2024, I decided to take some time off before looking for new opportunities. Once I started sending resumes and applications, like many of you, I never heard a thing. They went into an abyss with no communication whatsoever on any timely basis. When I did receive rejections I would always follow up to ask for any feedback that could be shared as to improve or understand what my resume did or didn’t have.

“Crickets” was all I ever got back.

Lately I have started to receive communications from jobs applied to and as usual I wrote back to ask for feedback. One company wrote back.

They indicated they were very impressed with my background and experience but went on to share with me two critical needs of the job which were not a part of my career journey or experience. While I was adjacent to these needs in other ways, they indicated they needed someone to have the exact experience so they could hit the ground running.

Their feedback was intelligent, clear and understandable. I thanked them for their feedback and actually told them I agreed with their assessment. I didn’t feel rejected, I didn’t take anything personally and I didn’t feel like my experience was being devalued.

What I felt was that this organization knew exactly what they needed, weren’t afraid to say so and could articulate in a way as to not discourage a potential future candidate.

For hiring managers and recruiters who follow my posts, listen up. This is what candidates really want. If they are not the right candidate for you but have taken the time to apply, let them know why. If candidates reach out for feedback, share feedback in a way that speaks to the needs of the job and not to lessen their value or experience or make them feel they shouldn’t have applied in the first place.

Tip for the Day - Feedback shared in an intelligent and timely manner goes a long way. If you do it well, you will be building a database of future potential candidates as well as customers of your products and believers in your brand.

🚨 Before You Get the Job Offer or Interview… You’ve Already Been Googled

Most candidates focus on:
📄 Resume
🎯 Interview answers
📊 Experience

But there’s something happening behind the scenes that impacts hiring decisions more than people realize.

💡 Here’s the reality:
Before interviews — and definitely before offers — recruiters and hiring managers are Googling you.

Not to dig for dirt.
But to avoid surprises. 🎯

📌 What actually gets checked
🔹 LinkedIn vs Resume
If titles, dates, or responsibilities don’t match — it creates doubt. 📊

And here’s something overlooked:
👉 Name consistency

HR departments and hiring managers have told me this directly.

👉 If your resume says: Tom Johnson
👉 Your email says: studmuffinTJ@gmail.com
👉 And LinkedIn says: William T. Johnson II

That creates confusion
👉 “Is this the same person?”
💡 Keep everything aligned.

🔹 Public Social Profiles
No one cares if you had a life.
But there’s a line:

🟢 Normal: friends, trips, social life
🔴 Risky: negativity, trashing employers
👉 Political rants fall here too.

Hiring managers think:

👉 “Will this create friction internally?”
💡 Sometimes the smartest move is to keep it private.

🔹 How You Talk About Work Online
❗ “I hate my boss”
❗ “This company is a joke”

Even if it’s old…
They assume you’ll do it again.

🔹 “Day in the Life” Work Content
Filming your job, posting internal content…

🚫 Raises confidentiality concerns
🚫 Can look like you’re not focused

Reality:
Nobody really cares… seriously, NOBODY cares
Except your employer. ⚡

🔹 Work Devices
Company devices aren’t private.
Certain behavior can get flagged:

🔸 Negative language
🔸 Questionable searches

Not common.
But it happens.

📈 What matters
This isn’t about being perfect.
It’s about being aware.

🟢 Smart play
✔ Keep profiles aligned
✔ Clean up obvious red flags
✔ Be careful with political content
✔ Don’t turn your job into content
✔ Assume anything public can be seen

🎯 Bottom line
Hiring decisions aren’t just based on interviews.
They’re influenced by what shows up before you even speak.

I run a team and I hire people.
And, I’m absolutely for this shift toward self-taught skills. I think you get a really interesting picture of people's grit & creativity by what they're teaching themselves.

FWIW... some of the most interesting candidates (young and old) I’ve seen lately are coming along that path.

People who are actively taking the initiative to learn something on their own... those who build, test, and figure new things out without being told exactly what to do; that matters a lot in my process.

But sitting on the hiring side, you do start to notice a pattern. While the number of skills people can list has exploded, the number of people who can clearly show how they use those skills isn’t keeping up. It’s never been easier to learn something. And, that’s a good thing. But, this also means people show up sounding more capable than they actually are.

So the job shifts.
You're not just asking what someone knows, but how deep can they go? How they think. Can they take a messy problem and put structure to it? Can they decide what matters and what doesn’t? Can they actually move something forward when there isn’t a clear playbook?

This is where the separation happens (at least for me). Candidates who stand out don’t overwhelm you with everything they’ve learned. When you test it, the qualified ones walk you through something real... what they were trying to do, where it got hard, what they chose to prioritize, what worked, what didn’t, and what they’d change if they had to do it again.

You can feel the difference pretty quick.

So for me, where someone has 'learned' or 'mastered' something has become a lot less important. At least on paper. I’m much more interested in whether they can apply it in a way that shows solid judgment [a word I'm hanging on these days.]

Because at this point, there's nothing but access to knowledge. Judgment is where the separation happens. And the people who can demonstrate that, regardless of background, are the ones I want on my team.
__

↳ ~92% say proof of application matters more than just listing skills

𝙒𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙗𝙚𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙖 𝙧𝙚𝙘𝙧𝙪𝙞𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙩𝙖𝙪𝙜𝙝𝙩 𝙢𝙚 𝙖𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙛𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚:

It’s not what most people think.

Working in recruitment, I speak to people every single day who are trying to prove themselves.

And the biggest misconception I see?

People think confidence is about being the loudest.

The most outgoing.
The best at “selling yourself.”
It’s not.

The candidates who actually get hired move differently.

They don’t rush to fill silence.
They don’t over-explain.
They don’t try to impress every second.

They’re just… clear.

Clear on what they’ve done.
Clear on what they want next.
And comfortable owning both.

Confidence, in reality, looks like:
• Saying less, but meaning it
• Not downplaying your achievements
• Being okay with not being “perfect”
• Letting your experience speak without overcompensating

I’ve seen incredibly talented engineers talk themselves out of opportunities just by softening everything they say.

“I just…”
“I only…”
“I was lucky to…”

No.

You led it.
You built it.
You delivered it.

Say it like that.

Because the truth is, in interviews and in business, people don’t just buy your experience.

They buy how certain you are about it.

97 people in only six days! 🏋🏼♂️ This is the number of people who requested my help with Annual Reviews, Interviews, and Career Development on LinkedIn alone.

I feel overwhelmed not because of the number of people I had to go through but because of what they request.

90% of the time, those who want to prepare for an annual review are also shaping up their CVs.

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗯𝗲 𝗮 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼:

👉🏻 Get to know your market value and how much raise you could ask/expect;

👉🏻 Feel more secure before the interview - no matter what, you have a back-up plan;

👉🏻 Build confidence - having initial interviews, you get to practice answering sometimes uncomfortable questions.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹:

🔥 Looking for something else before the annual review - you may lose your focus, and that may lead to mistakes and wrong decisions and then affect your review;

🔥 Commitment & loyalty - are you really committed to the brand / company? You may send wrong signals if you start challenging the status quo;

🔥 The chances are that you may talk with your colleague about your doubts, and doubts spread like fire. Soon the whole floor may start doubting the leadership or themselves. Demotivation spreads, and that affects overall performance.

𝗦𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘄𝗲 𝗱𝗼?

𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 - do not wait for 12 months to check on your employees; remember to review their GOALS and address performance and what could be done better every quarter. It is really not so hard to pull up your employees’ Personal Development Plan and cross-check where they are every few months. And if you were not there for the entire 12 months, speak to the peers, do a proper 360.

𝗘𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀 - instead of spreading fire in the office, remember why you joined the company in the first place. Divorcing the company is easy. However, if that happens often, the common denominator is… you. Which means you are also the solution.

"So, Tanya... why haven't I heard back yet?" (Sent 2 hours after the interview) 🚩

The Hook: I’ve spent years in the "original HR" trenches, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some candidate questions simply don’t make sense in 2026.

We all want the job. We all want the salary. But often, the questions we ask reveal a lack of Executive Presence and Strategic Thinking. ### The "Nonsensical" Top 3 (And why they stall your career):

1. "What did the other candidate have that I didn't?" 🕵️♀️

Hiring isn't a math equation. It’s about chemistry and cultural fit. Comparing yourself to a stranger is irrelevant. The only question that matters is: "Did I bridge the gap between my resume and the company's problem?"

2. "What does your company actually do?" 🔍

In an era where Google is free and LinkedIn is a goldmine, asking this in an interview tells me you aren't looking for a career—you’re just looking for a paycheck.

3. "How soon can I get a promotion?" 📈

I love ambition. But asking about the "exit" before you’ve even mastered the "entrance" signals that you aren't focused on delivering value today.

The "Beyond the Resume" Reality:

As a Communication Specialist, I now look at these questions through a different lens. It’s not just what you ask; it’s the vocalics, the body language, and the timing. A "nonsensical" question usually stems from a lack of preparation. When you don't know your own value proposition, you end up asking HR to be your career counselor.

The Shift: Stop asking "What can you do for me?" and start asking questions that prove you are a Solution Provider.Recruiters, what is the one question that always makes you tilt your head in an interview? Candidates, what's the one thing you're always dying to ask but are afraid to? Let's settle it in the comments! 👇
